```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
has_tna <- requireNamespace("tna", quietly = TRUE)
has_traminer <- requireNamespace("TraMineR", quietly = TRUE)
has_nestimate <- requireNamespace("Nestimate", quietly = TRUE)
```

A prediction suffix tree is estimated from ordered categorical sequences:
for every position of every sequence, the state that occurs and the states
that precede it. The same sequences reach an analysis in several shapes. A
panel study stores one row per person and one column per time point; a
learning platform or a coding scheme produces an event log with one row per
event, a person, a time stamp and a code; and a sequence or network analysis
that is already under way holds the sequences inside a fitted object.
`context_tree()` accepts each of these shapes and reduces them to the same
internal list of sequences, so that the tree does not depend on the route
by which the data arrived.

This guide describes each input route, the rules by which an event log is
cut into sequences, the treatment of missing values, and the hand-off from
objects of the `tna`, `Nestimate` and `TraMineR` packages. Each section
confirms that two routes to the same sequences give the same tree.
[A complete workflow](workflow.html) shows the analysis that follows.

```{r package}
library(transitiontrees)
```

## Data

The package bundles four example datasets, two in each shape.

- **`trajectories`** — a wide character matrix: 138 learners (rows) by 15
  time steps (columns), with the states `Active`, `Average` and
  `Disengaged`; trailing `NA`s mark the end of a learner's record.
- **`engagement`** — a wide data frame: 1,000 students by 25 weeks
  (`T1` to `T25`) over the same three states; synthetic data from the `tna`
  package.
- **`group_regulation_long`** — an event log of 27,533 collaborative
  regulation moves: the student (`Actor`), the time stamp (`Time`,
  POSIXct), the move (`Action`, nine codes), and the covariates
  `Achiever`, `Group` and `Course`; synthetic data from the `tna` package.
- **`ai_long`** — an event log of 8,551 coded moves from projects in which
  people worked with an AI assistant: the project (`project`), an explicit
  session identifier (`session_id`), a Unix time stamp (`timestamp`), the
  move (`code`, eight codes), the order of the move within its session
  (`order_in_session`), and a coarser grouping of the codes (`cluster`).

## Wide sequences

In the wide shape each row is one sequence and each column one position,
read from left to right. A character matrix and a data frame are read in
the same way.

```{r wide}
head(engagement, 3)
from_frame <- context_tree(engagement, max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
from_matrix <- context_tree(as.matrix(engagement), max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
from_frame
identical(as.data.frame(from_frame), as.data.frame(from_matrix))
```

The tree is fitted on 1,000 sequences and 24,555 observed states, and the
two containers give identical pathway tables. A sequence may end early:
the `NA` cells after the last observed state are dropped, so sequences of
different lengths need no padding rule. In `trajectories`, two of the 138
rows contain no observed state at all and do not form a sequence.

```{r trajectories}
context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 1, min_count = 5)
```

The banner reports 136 sequences and 1,870 observations.

Numeric matrices are refused. In the sibling network packages a square
numeric matrix denotes a transition matrix, and a sequence coded by
integers must be converted to character states explicitly, so that the
alphabet is never inferred from numbers by accident. The refusal is a
classed error, `transitiontrees_bad_input`.

```{r numeric, error = TRUE}
context_tree(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2))
```

## Lists of sequences

A list of character vectors holds one sequence per element. The elements
may differ in length.

```{r list}
sessions <- list(c("plan", "discuss", "consensus", "plan"),
                 c("monitor", "discuss", "plan"),
                 c("plan", "plan", "consensus", "discuss", "plan"))
context_tree(sessions, max_depth = 1, min_count = 1)
```

The three sequences contribute 12 observed states over four codes.

## Missing values and void codes

In wide and list input four codes mark the absence of an observation: `NA`,
the empty string `""`, and the `TraMineR` codes `"%"` (void, the position
after the end of a sequence) and `"*"` (missing). A cell with any of them
is dropped, the observed states on either side are joined, and the code
never becomes a state of the alphabet. The two frames below hold the same
observed states, one with gap codes and one without.

```{r missing}
with_gaps <- data.frame(T1 = c("A", "B", "A"),
                        T2 = c("%", "B", "*"),
                        T3 = c("B", "", "A"),
                        T4 = c(NA, "%", "%"))
without_gaps <- data.frame(T1 = c("A", "B", "A"),
                           T2 = c("B", "B", "A"))
identical(as.data.frame(context_tree(with_gaps, max_depth = 1, min_count = 1)),
          as.data.frame(context_tree(without_gaps, max_depth = 1, min_count = 1)))
```

Dropping an internal gap joins the states on either side of it, which
creates a transition that was not observed. When gaps inside sequences are
frequent, `impute_sequences()` fills them from a fitted tree instead (see
[prediction and scoring](prediction-and-scoring.html)).

## Event logs

An event log has one row per event. `prepare_input()` turns it into the
wide shape: the events of each `actor` are ordered by `time` (or by an
`order` column) and are cut into sessions wherever the gap between
consecutive events exceeds `time_threshold` seconds (default 900, that is,
15 minutes). Each session becomes one row; the columns are `T1`, `T2`, and
so on.

```{r prepare}
wide <- prepare_input(group_regulation_long,
                      actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action")
dim(wide)
subset(head(wide, 3), select = T1:T8)
```

The 27,533 events form 2,000 sessions, one per student, the longest with 26
moves; the first eight positions of three sessions are shown. The row
names identify the student and the session. Naming `action` in `context_tree()` performs the same reshaping
before fitting, so the two routes give the same tree.

```{r long-equal}
from_log <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                         actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                         max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
from_wide <- context_tree(wide, max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
identical(as.data.frame(from_log), as.data.frame(from_wide))
```

### The session threshold

The threshold decides what counts as one sequence, and a transition is
counted only within a session. It should be chosen from the meaning of a
pause in the data rather than from its effect on the results. The number of
sessions under three thresholds:

```{r thresholds}
vapply(c(300, 900, 3600), \(seconds)
       nrow(prepare_input(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor",
                          time = "Time", action = "Action",
                          time_threshold = seconds)),
       integer(1))
```

A threshold of five minutes cuts the moves of the 2,000 students into
12,305 sessions; 15 minutes and one hour leave one session per student.

### Covariates of a sequence

A covariate recorded on the events, such as `Achiever`, describes the
sequence as a whole. `prepare_input(meta = )` carries the named columns
through the reshaping, one value per session taken from its first event.
`context_tree()` uses the same mechanism when `group` names a column of the
log, and fits one tree per group over a shared alphabet.

```{r group}
by_achievement <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                               actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                               action = "Action", group = "Achiever",
                               max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
summary(by_achievement)
```

Each achievement group holds 1,000 sessions. [Comparing
groups](comparing-groups.html) continues from such a grouped fit.

### Unix time and explicit sessions

A numeric time column is read as Unix time in seconds; `unix_time_unit`
selects milliseconds or microseconds, and `format` parses a character time
stamp. In `ai_long` the time stamp records the day of a session only:
every event of a day carries the same value. Splitting by time therefore
makes one sequence per project and day, with the events of a day kept in
the order of `order_in_session`.

```{r ai-time}
by_day <- prepare_input(ai_long, actor = "project", time = "timestamp",
                        order = "order_in_session", action = "code")
dim(by_day)
```

The log also records the session in which each move was made. Naming it in
`session` takes the sessions directly from that column, without
time-based splitting.

```{r ai-session}
by_session <- prepare_input(ai_long, actor = "project",
                            session = "session_id",
                            order = "order_in_session", action = "code")
dim(by_session)
```

The 8,551 moves form 160 project-days but 428 sessions. When the data
record sessions, the recorded session is the better unit: a project-day
joins the last move of one session to the first move of the next. The tree
is fitted from the log in the same way.

```{r ai-tree}
ai_tree <- context_tree(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                        order = "order_in_session", action = "code",
                        max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
state_frequencies(ai_tree)
```

`Execute` and `Investigate` account for 38% and 27% of the moves; `Ask` and
`Report` for about 1% and 2%.

## Objects from tna

A `tna` model keeps the sequences from which it was estimated.
`context_tree()` reads them from the model and decodes them through the
model's labels, so that the tree uses the same states as the network.

```{r tna-model, eval = has_tna}
engagement_tna <- tna::tna(engagement)
from_tna <- context_tree(engagement_tna, max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
identical(as.data.frame(from_frame), as.data.frame(from_tna))
```

An event log prepared by `tna::prepare_data()` can be passed to
`context_tree()` directly; the wide sequences it holds are used.
`prepare_data()` reports its session rule in messages, which are not shown
here. The tree is the same as the one fitted from the log directly: the
distance between the two trees is zero and their fit statistics agree.

```{r tna-prepared, eval = has_tna, message = FALSE}
prepared <- tna::prepare_data(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor",
                              time = "Time", action = "Action")
from_prepared <- context_tree(prepared, max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
tree_distance(from_log, from_prepared)
all.equal(model_fit(from_log), model_fit(from_prepared))
```

A grouped `tna` model fits one tree per group.

```{r tna-group, eval = has_tna}
from_group_model <- context_tree(tna::group_model(prepared, group = "Achiever"),
                                 max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
summary(from_group_model)
```

The two trees are those of the `group = "Achiever"` fit above.

A network estimated from a transition matrix alone carries no sequences.
The sequences cannot be recovered from aggregated transition weights, and
`context_tree()` refuses such an object with a `transitiontrees_bad_input`
error rather than fabricating sequences.

```{r tna-graph, eval = has_tna, error = TRUE}
states <- c("Active", "Average", "Disengaged")
weights <- matrix(c(0.6, 0.3, 0.1,
                    0.2, 0.5, 0.3,
                    0.1, 0.3, 0.6), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(states, states))
context_tree(tna::tna(weights))
```

## Objects from Nestimate

`Nestimate::build_tna()` and the other `build_*()` constructors return a
`netobject` that also keeps its sequences and a table of node labels, and a
grouped construction returns a `netobject_group`. `context_tree()` reads
both in the same way as the `tna` objects. The chunk below runs when
Nestimate is installed; it prints `TRUE` when the two routes give the same
pathway table.

```{r nestimate, eval = has_nestimate}
engagement_net <- Nestimate::build_tna(engagement)
from_nestimate <- context_tree(engagement_net, max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
identical(as.data.frame(from_frame), as.data.frame(from_nestimate))
```

## State sequence objects from TraMineR

A `TraMineR` state sequence object (class `stslist`) is a data frame of
states in which the end of a shorter sequence is filled with the void code
`"%"`. `context_tree()` reads the object, or the character matrix from
`as.matrix()`, and drops the void and missing codes.

`seqdef()` describes the states it found in messages, which are not shown.

```{r traminer, eval = has_traminer, message = FALSE}
engagement_seq <- TraMineR::seqdef(engagement)
from_stslist <- context_tree(engagement_seq, max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
from_seq_matrix <- context_tree(as.matrix(engagement_seq),
                                max_depth = 2, min_count = 5)
identical(as.data.frame(from_frame), as.data.frame(from_stslist))
identical(as.data.frame(from_frame), as.data.frame(from_seq_matrix))
```

Both routes give the tree fitted from the wide data frame, with no alphabet
to declare and no void code to remove by hand.

```{r restore-options, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
